description: Bacterial fruit blotch (BFB) is a destructive bacterial disease affecting cucurbit crops worldwide. It is caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Acidovorax citrulli and spreads primarily through contaminated seeds. The disease can cause severe economic losses, particularly in watermelon and melon production. Infection leads to water-soaked lesions on seedlings, leaves, and fruits, eventually resulting in fruit rot, cracking, and crop loss. Because the bacterium can survive inside seeds for many years, disease control mainly relies on seed sanitation and strict hygiene practices.
symptoms_and_damage: Seedlings: water-soaked lesions on cotyledons and hypocotyls leading to collapse and death
Leaves: large irregular lesions that are brown to black in watermelon and reddish-brown in melon
Leaf lesions often spread along the main midrib
Fruits: small water-soaked lesions that enlarge and become sunken
Fruit rind becomes necrotic, leading to cracking and decay
Lesions allow secondary infections by other pathogens
Severely infected fruits rot and may contaminate seeds
disease_cycle: Primary transmission occurs through infected seeds
The bacterium can survive inside seeds for many years
Initially behaves as a saprophyte using nutrients from the seed
Switches to pathogenic growth when the seedling emerges
Bacteria infect developing fruit through stomata 3–4 weeks after fruit set
Symptoms often appear late, near harvest, creating a delay between infection and detection
Infected fruits may contaminate new seeds, continuing the cycle
favorable_conditions: High bacterial load on contaminated seeds
Dense plant populations and overhead irrigation
prevention_and_cultural_controls: Conduct seed health testing before planting
Maintain strict sanitation in nurseries and greenhouses
Reduce overhead irrigation to limit bacterial spread
Remove infected plant debris and volunteer cucurbit plants
chemical_control: Copper-based bactericides may be used preventively to reduce bacterial spread
Chemical control is generally limited in effectiveness
Applications should follow local agricultural regulations and product labels
biological_control: No widely established biological control methods are currently available
Research is ongoing to identify effective biological antagonists
resistance_breeding: No commercial cultivars with strong resistance are currently available
Some experimental watermelon and melon accessions have shown partial resistance
Breeding programs continue to search for resistant germplasm
monitoring: Inspect seedlings for water-soaked lesions on cotyledons
Monitor leaves for irregular brown or black lesions along veins
Check fruits for water-soaked spots that enlarge and become sunken
Test seed lots for contamination before planting
direct_control_and_restrictions: Destroy infected plants to prevent spread
Use heat treatment of seeds (around 85°C for 3–5 days) to reduce bacterial contamination
Implement strict hygiene in seed production and transplant facilities
Avoid saving seeds from infected fruits
